item.title: Fortran cells
item.description:
A ```fortran block is a Fortran cell (checked since go-notebook v0.16.0, run since v0.17.0). The Fortran is go-embedded-fortran (v0.17.0), a pure-Go Fortran: no external compiler is started. Its sema session checks the cell and gives the names and the errors, its eval.Session runs it. A cell is a program’s loose material and units alike: declarations and statements at top level, subroutines, functions, modules, derived types, even a program. Free form, implicit typing off.

Cells share one session

A notebook with Fortran cells makes the worker import go-notebook’s fcells package, which owns one eval.Session. A Fortran cell sees the variables (with the values the earlier cells left), procedures, modules and derived types of the Fortran cells before it, in notebook order: n = n + 1 in a cell after the one that has integer :: n = 3 changes the same n. A cell with an error leaves nothing behind for the next ones. Names are case-insensitive. Redefinition shadows in Fortran (a cell that runs again defines a new version that later cells see); between two cells of the notebook it is refused, as go-notebook’s rule of one definition per name.

The names a cell reads from earlier Fortran cells are its uses and give the graph its edges: a variable, a procedure, a derived type named in a declaration and a module named in use all do.

Fortran variables stay in Fortran

They are not shared with Go, Ruby, Julia, R or C cells in either direction yet (analysis.Isolated, as R’s): a Go cell that reads a Fortran name finds it undefined, and a Fortran cell does not see a Go variable. A result reaches the reader as printed text; a cell shows text only.

Output and errors

What a cell prints is its output; standard error and the text of STOP are its standard error; STOP ends the cell, not the session. A refused cell or a failure is reported at line L, column C of the cell, and a cell that fails while it runs keeps what it had done.

Limits

A notebook may come from anyone. A cell may make at most 2^32 DO iterations and procedure calls, run 30 s, and the evaluator’s own bounds apply: 2^28 elements per array, 2^26 characters per string, 2^15 nested calls. Output is cut at 16 MiB per stream. The step count, not a timer, is what ends a loop in WebAssembly. --timeout and --memory apply as to every cell and kill the worker, session included. INCLUDE is refused: no file is read.

What the evaluator refuses

It says so, positioned: type extension and select type, pointer components, vector subscripts, elsewhere, dim= and mask=, complex variables, character arrays, read from a unit, and an array declared with an initialisation.

The playground

Fortran cells run in the browser playground, with no server and no compiler: the evaluator is linked into the playground’s second WebAssembly core (the one it loads for a notebook with a Fortran, R, Ruby or Julia cell), through fcells.Session.Eval; the default core stays Go-only. The playground bounds a cell tighter than the kernel does: 200 million DO iterations and procedure calls, 10 s and 16 MiB of output per stream. An endless do ends with step limit reached: the cell ran too many loop iterations and calls and the page stays usable. The second core grew by 1.3 MB (0.28 MB gzipped).

examples/fortran.md runs end to end: notebook run examples/fortran.md.
